title: The Server Is a Country
subtitle: A Social History of Life Inside the Virtual World
description: Between 1999 and today, tens of millions of people inhabited persistent digital societies that developed their own economies, laws, and mourning rituals. These were not mere games but sovereign territories where guilds operated as workplaces with performance reviews, virtual plagues generated real epidemiological data, and banking collapses prompted player-written constitutions. Drawing on chat logs, patch notes, and forum archives, this history reconstructs the ordinary evenings of a civilization that existed only while servers remained paid. From the corpse runs of EverQuest to the gold farmers whose labor was essential yet denied citizenship, these pages document a society built from code and sustained by human connection. Here are the funerals held for players who died offline, the scandals that forced new laws, and the historians preserving worlds now gone dark. A definitive record of communities that flourished in the glow of monitors, proving that wherever people gather, they inevitably build a country.

editorReview.text: This chronicle of digital societies shines when it delves into the granular, lived experience of its subjects. The early chapters deliver on their promise of a modern 'Montaillou,' where a player's corpse run becomes a poignant study of virtual inheritance and a guild's DKP spreadsheet is convincingly analyzed as a foundational constitution. However, the book's structural integrity wavers as it progresses. The introduction of a second major game world feels abrupt and disrupts the immersive, single-domain focus established at the outset.
